continuity_scope: 上橋菜穂子 (Nahoko Uehashi), 『精霊の守り人』 (Seirei no Moribito), 偕成社 first hardcover, July 1996, ISBN 9784035401506, 326 pages. The English title Moribito: Guardian of the Spirit is Cathy Hirano's authorized translation under a distinct 2008 Scholastic/Arthur A. Levine edition. This audit reads the 1996 Japanese novel as canon and uses the official English translation only for transparent localization support; it does not merge anime, manga, live action, later novels, guides, or adaptations.

coverage_rule: Include the adult bodyguard Balsa, Prince Chagum, Balsa's two named support-network figures Tanda and Torogai, the named court investigator Shuga, Balsa's named deceased mentor Jiguro, and the individual ruler identified by the title Mikado/帝. This seven-person cohort covers the protagonist/protected child, independent protectors/knowledge holders, the court investigation and persecution, and the formative mentor. Other named guards, hunters, villagers, court officials, spirits, and historical figures are omitted.
omissions: All later Moribito/Tabibito books, guidebooks, short fiction, anime, manga, live action, games, interviews, and adaptations.
Named but non-cohort hunters, imperial officials, palace staff, villagers, spirits, animals, and historical figures.
New Yogo, peoples, court offices, the spirit realm, spirits as categories, magic, the egg, weapons, places, and cultural inspirations as character nodes.
uncertainties: Japanese source spellings/scripts and authorized English-localization forms may differ. Japanese script, Hepburn romanization, and English translation aliases are retained rather than assumed interchangeable across editions.

The official Japanese and English descriptions support the core premise; copyright-limited witnesses make a full claim-by-claim searchable text unavailable here. Sequence locators identify the primary-novel scenes, while terms whose exact novel definition cannot be confirmed are marked needs-review.

New Yogo and the novel's social/cosmological material are fictional. They may invite comparative discussion, but are not claims about Japanese, East Asian, indigenous, or any other real culture/religion.
The novel includes attempted killing of a child, state violence, combat, death, traumatic memory, and political coercion. Records state these non-graphically.
evidence_basis: The stated 1996 Japanese novel is the canonical witness. Kaiseisha official book/series pages establish title, edition, first-novel status, Balsa, Chagum, New Yogo, the imperial pursuit, and the spirit egg. ALA's record identifies the authorized Cathy Hirano translation and English localization. The seven-record audit remains deliberately narrow where detailed primary text is not publicly searchable.
